svg.title: Sigstore keyless signing, from OIDC authentication to a verifiable bundle
svg.desc: Six steps. First, the build runner authenticates to an OIDC provider and receives an identity token describing the workflow. Second, it generates an ephemeral key pair in memory on the runner. Third, Fulcio validates the token and issues an X.509 certificate valid for about ten minutes, binding the ephemeral public key to the verified identity in the certificate's subject alternative name. Fourth, the runner signs the artifact digest and submits the entry to the Rekor transparency log, which returns an inclusion proof against a co-signed checkpoint. Fifth, the client obtains an RFC 3161 signed timestamp from a trusted timestamp authority, because Rekor version 2 no longer returns Signed Entry Timestamps or integrated time. Sixth, the resulting bundle carries the certificate, signature, inclusion proof, and timestamp, and the private key is discarded. A footer notes that the ten-minute certificate is why the timestamp matters, since verification must establish that the signature existed while the certificate was valid.
svg.text: Keyless signing: nothing durable is ever held
The signing key exists only for the length of one build step, so there is no key to store, rotate, or steal.
STEP 1
Authenticate the workload
The runner obtains an OIDC identity token
from its CI platform, naming the repository,
workflow file, and ref that is building.
STEP 2
Generate an ephemeral key pair
Created in memory on the runner. It is never
written to a secret store and never reused
by a second build.
STEP 3 · FULCIO
Issue a 10-minute certificate
Fulcio validates the token and binds the
ephemeral public key to the verified identity
in the certificate's SAN.
STEP 4 · REKOR
Sign, then log the entry
The runner signs the artifact digest and
submits the entry. Rekor returns an inclusion
proof against a co-signed checkpoint.
STEP 5 · TIMESTAMP AUTHORITY
Obtain an RFC 3161 timestamp
Rekor v2 no longer returns Signed Entry
Timestamps or integrated time. Sigstore operates
timestamp.sigstore.dev
RESULT
One verifiable bundle
Certificate, signature, inclusion proof, and
timestamp travel together. The private key is
discarded: nothing to rotate or revoke.
The ten-minute certificate is why the timestamp matters: by the time anyone verifies, the certificate has long expired, so verification must
establish that the signature existed while it was still valid. That is what the log inclusion proof and the RFC 3161 timestamp jointly provide.
